transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-10-12
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Evan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Jared (Northstar Platform), Monica (Northstar SRE), Aaron (Northstar CTO)
Links shared: https://redwood.app/notes/northstar-burst-2027-10-12, Grafana: https://grafana.northstar.local/d/redwood/burst-1

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be fuzzy):
- Reviewed last week's pilot numbers: steady-state 180 rps, peak bursts ~520 rps for short windows.
- Discussed continuous batching improvements and KV cache warmup strategy; agreed to run an extended burst test.
- Agreed action items for Redwood to run tests and for Northstar to provide traffic traces.

Transcript:
[00:00] Evan: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick roll call — priya with me from Redwood, and i think we have jared, monica, and aaron from northstar. can you hear ok?
[00:10] Jared: Yep, loud and clear.
[00:12] Monica: Good, thanks.
[00:15] Evan: Cool — objective for today is tight: review throughput from the last week, validate whether the continuous batching change helped, and decide next steps for burst capacity testing.
[00:25] Priya: I'll start with the numbers i pulled this morning. so steady state we've been seeing about 180 rps, median latency at 95th is ~280ms with our small model variant. During the synthetic spike on tuesday you folks hit ~520 rps for about 70 seconds, we saw a sharp drop in KV cache hit rate during that spike — down to 23% from typical 68%.
[00:45] Jared: yeah that matches our logs. i think the cache cold-start was the big issue — we have a lot of unique user prompts during the spike window.
[00:52] Priya: right, and the continuous batching tweak we rolled out cut the per-token overhead by ~12% on average in our bench runs. but in the real traffic the benefit is gated by cache hit rate and queueing collapse when concurrency crosses the threshold.
[01:10] Aaron: can you clarify queueing collapse? like are you seeing head-of-line blocking or something else?
[01:15] Priya: good question. what we've observed is that once concurrency goes above ~12 concurrent model contexts on a single worker, the scheduler starts to favor latency SLOs and batches shrink, which increases per-token cost and reduces throughput efficiency — that shows up as an apparent collapse in throughput for a few seconds while the autoscaler re-balances. it's not classical head-of-line but a scheduling granularity artifact.
[01:40] Monica: so above 12 concurrent contexts per GPU we lose efficiency — can we set a cap? we prefer predictable latency.
[01:46] Evan: yes, you can set concurrency targets per route in the config. for the pilot we recommended 8-10 for the small model variant to avoid that collapse. but that trades off peak capacity.
[02:00] Jared: what about dedicated pool? if we go dedicated, can we push that concurrency higher?
[02:06] Priya: dedicated gives you more predictable throughput because pool isolation reduces noisy neighbor effects and you can tune instance types. you still hit the scheduling granularity limits per GPU, but with dedicated you can increase the number of workers rather than pushing per-worker concurrency, which usually preserves batching efficiency.
[02:25] Aaron: cost question — beefing up dedicated to handle your peaks looks expensive. is there a hybrid approach?
[02:30] Evan: yes hybrid is common: reserved dedicated capacity for steady state, with hosted burst credits or autoscaler burst capacity for occasional peaks. Redwood offers burst credits as an add-on so you pay for short high-throughput windows without committing to double the fleet.
[02:48] Monica: how do rollbacks look if burst causes regressions? we need a safe canary.
[02:52] Priya: built-in canary and automatic fallback exist — you can set a fallback model (e.g., smaller quantized variant) and a region fallback. the control plane can route to the fallback if latency or error rate exceeds thresholds. we can demo the rollback sequence in the canary run.
[03:10] Evan: ok let's look at the concrete tests. priya, what do you propose?
[03:14] Priya: two tests: 1) an extended 4-hour burst run at 2x baseline concurrency but with KV cache warmup phase; 2) a short 20-minute stress at 3x with aggressive queueing to see where tail latency breaks. for test 1 we'll warm the prefix cache by replaying top prompt families for 30 minutes before the burst. that should simulate a warmed-prod scenario.
[03:37] Jared: replaying prompts — we'll need to sanitise traces. we can produce the top 10 prompt families but need to scrub PII.
[03:44] Monica: and can we run the burst in our staging region to avoid touching prod?
[03:47] Priya: staging is fine but note staging hardware variance can change numbers; best is staging with the same instance types and networking profile.
[03:56] Aaron: what's the rollback latency if a model variant hits errors mid-burst? like how quickly will traffic flip?
[04:02] Priya: automatic fallback is near-real-time; flip is usually within 20-45 seconds depending on propagation and open connections. we have tracing to show the switch.
[04:12] Evan: budget-wise, we've estimated the 4-hour burst will use ~120k tokens and trigger 2x concurrency across 6 workers — we'll attach a cost estimate in the follow-up.
[04:23] Jared: can you confirm whether the KV cache is per-worker or global? our architecture assumed a global cache across the pool.
[04:29] Priya: current pilot uses worker-local KV cache plus a shared prefix index. it's close to hybrid. sometimes the transcriber logs say "K V cash" which is weird — but in practice each worker keeps a hot cache and the control plane routes likely cache hits to warmed workers where possible.
[04:46] Monica: that's interesting — routing to warmed workers could help a lot. are there metrics for cache warm routing?
[04:50] Priya: yes we have a route-level metric "cache_routed_pct" in Grafana. last week it averaged 42% during normal traffic, dropped to 18% during spike.
[04:59] Jared: okay, so the warmup will try to get that to 60-70% ideally.
[05:03] Priya: right. if we can bump warm routing to 60% the effective throughput improves a lot because more requests hit the hot path and batches stay larger.
[05:12] Aaron: any security flags with replaying traces for warmup?
[05:16] Evan: you control what gets replayed; redact PII, use hashed user IDs. Redwood's private deploy supports on-prem replay if you prefer. also SOC 2 and SSO integration are in our security pack.
[05:29] Monica: we will need SOC 2 docs before any dedicated purchase.
[05:33] Evan: noted — i'll attach SOC 2 + ISO docs in the follow-up.
[05:36] Priya: quick aside: we also have an adaptive batching algo in beta that expands batch window slightly when queue depth is high; it trades a few ms of added latency for substantially higher throughput efficiency. i can enable it for the 4-hour test if you want to experiment.
[05:55] Jared: yes enable it, but only as an A/B against a control run. we need to know impact on tail latency.
[06:02] Priya: will do. we'll run parallel runs with and without adaptive batching and compare 95/99 latencies and cost per token.
[06:10] Monica: what instrumentation will you provide? we need raw traces, token-level cost breakdown, and concurrency histograms.
[06:16] Priya: we'll share a Grafana board with per-route rps, latency buckets (p50/p95/p99), batch size distribution, KV cache hit rate, and cost per token. link in notes.
[06:24] Evan: also we'll annotate the run with rollouts and any fallback events so you can correlate spikes.
[06:30] Jared: timeline — can we run the 4-hour burst next thursday? that's 2027-10-15 in our timezone.
[06:35] Priya: we can schedule that. prefer to do it early morning 08:00 PT to capture lower background noise.
[06:42] Aaron: one more on fallback: if the fallback model reduces quality, do we have a canary QA guard? we can't tolerate degraded correctness for more than a minute in some user flows.
[06:54] Priya: you can set a quality guard using eval prompts — the control plane evaluates a small sample of outputs and if semantic similarity drops below threshold, it pauses fallback or reduces route rate. it's not perfect but has worked in other pilots.
[07:10] Monica: good — send docs on the eval guard mechanism.
[07:14] Evan: noted. i'll include a short runbook for canary + rollback and the semantic guard.
[07:20] (crosstalk/indistinct) Speaker 1: uhhm yeah
[07:25] Priya: quick note on concurrency targets: set your route to 9 concurrent contexts for steady state; set a burst policy to allow temporary 18 concurrency on a controlled fleet with warmup. that gives you headroom but prevents the scheduler collapse we saw at 12 on mixed fleets.
[07:46] Jared: 18 seems high but ok during educated bursts. how does that map to worker count?
[07:51] Priya: depends on model size; for your small variant that's roughly 3-4 model contexts per GPU, so 18 concurrency across the fleet might be 6 GPUs. we'll surface an exact mapping in the follow-up.
[08:03] Evan: now let's look at the week-over-week numbers: Priya, can you summarize delta since we changed batching?
[08:08] Priya: sure — continuous batching decreased average batch creation latency by 9ms and increased average batch size by 6% in the bench. in production visible effects were muted because of cache churn. overall throughput up ~7% across the week, cost/unit down ~4% where caches were warm.
[08:26] Monica: were there any error spikes?
[08:28] Priya: small uptick in transient 503s during two minute rebalances on tuesday; autoscaler handled it quickly.
[08:33] Jared: what caused the rebalances?
[08:35] Priya: autoscaler reacted to network jitter plus a worker OOM on one node. we've patched the OOM vector and suggested a different memory headroom config.
[08:45] Aaron: can you share that headroom config? we run strict memory limits.
[08:48] Priya: yes — i'll include recommended worker memory reserve in the follow-up; reduce oom risk by reserving ~8% more GPU memory for KV structures.
[08:58] Evan: ok, let's capture concrete acceptance criteria for the pilot success: 1) sustain 2x baseline for 4 hours with mean latency <350ms p95 <450ms and cache routed pct >55%; 2) cost delta vs baseline below 1.8x; 3) canary rollback works within 60s. agreeable?
[09:22] Aaron: those look reasonable, assuming the quality guard holds.
[09:26] Jared: yes we accept, provided we get the Grafana dashboards and the runbook.
[09:30] Evan: summary of next steps — i'll email SOC 2 + runbook and updated pricing; priya will schedule the tests and run them; jared to provide traces.
[09:40] Monica: small ask — can Redwood share a short notebook of how you calculate cost per token for mixed batching? our finance folks want the model.
[09:46] Priya: sure, we'll attach a cost-model notebook (CSV + explanation).
[09:50] Evan: final question — any blockers from your side?
[09:53] Jared: only trace export scrubbing — will take a day.
[09:56] Aaron: none from exec side.
[09:58] Evan: sweet. we'll run the 4-hour burst on 2027-10-15 08:00 PT. priya will share calendar invite and dashboard. evan to follow up with pricing + security pack. jared to upload traces by 10/18.
[10:12] (meeting closing) Speaker 2: thanks everyone, bye

End of transcript.
